content: Write a letter of recommendation for a student applying to graduate school.

Below is a complete, adaptable letter of recommendation. Replace the bracketed text with specifics — the more concrete detail you add (project names, grades, class rank, anecdotes), the more persuasive it becomes.

---

**[Your Name]**
[Title, e.g., Associate Professor of Chemistry]
[Department], [Institution]
[Address] | [Email] | [Phone]

[Date]

**Re: Letter of Recommendation for [Student Name]**

Graduate Admissions Committee
[Program Name]
[University Name]

Dear Members of the Admissions Committee:

It is my great pleasure to recommend [Student Name] for admission to the [Ph.D./M.S./M.A.] program in [Field] at [University]. I have known [Student] for [number] years, first as a student in my [Course Name and Number] course and subsequently as an undergraduate researcher in my laboratory. In that time, [he/she/they] has proven to be among the most capable and self-directed students I have worked with, and I recommend [him/her/them] without reservation.

**Academic Ability**

[Student] enrolled in my [Course Name], a [upper-division/graduate-level] course of [number] students, and earned [a grade of A / the highest final grade in the class]. What distinguished [him/her/them] was not simply the grade but the quality of [his/her/their] thinking. On the final project, which asked students to [brief description of assignment], [Student] [describe what they did that was unusually strong — e.g., "went well beyond the assigned framework to incorporate a Bayesian treatment of measurement uncertainty, an approach we had not covered in class"]. [He/She/They] also had a habit of asking the kind of question that reframed a discussion for the entire room — the sort of intellectual instinct that cannot be taught and that I associate with students who go on to do excellent independent work.

Across [his/her/their] transcript, [Student] has compiled a [GPA] GPA while taking a demanding load that includes [list 2–3 rigorous courses]. [Optional: If there is a weakness — a low grade, a semester dip — address it briefly and constructively here.]

**Research Experience**

[Student] joined my research group in [semester/year] and has worked with me on [project title or topic]. [He/She/They] took primary responsibility for [specific task or component], which required [specific skills — e.g., "learning to operate our confocal microscope, writing image-segmentation code in Python, and troubleshooting a persistent sample-contamination problem that had stalled the project for months"].

I want to highlight one episode in particular. [Describe a specific challenge and how the student handled it — e.g., "When our initial hypothesis failed to hold up across three replicate trials, [Student] did not wait for direction. [He/She/They] independently reviewed the recent literature, identified a plausible confounding variable we had overlooked, and designed a control experiment that confirmed the alternative explanation. That insight redirected the project and became the basis of our current manuscript."] This is exactly the resilience and initiative that doctoral research demands.

[Student]'s work has resulted in [co-authorship on a manuscript currently under review at [Journal] / a poster presented at [Conference] / an honors thesis titled "[Title]"]. [He/She/They] presented this work at [venue] and handled questioning from faculty with a poise and command of the material that would not have been out of place from a senior graduate student.

**Personal Qualities and Collaboration**

Beyond technical skill, [Student] is a genuinely good colleague. [He/She/They] mentored [number] junior students in the lab, patiently teaching [specific protocol or skill], and is the person other students seek out when they are stuck. [He/She/They] receives criticism gracefully and acts on it — a quality I do not take for granted. [Optional: note relevant context, e.g., "[Student] has accomplished all of this while working [number] hours per week to support [himself/herself/themselves] and while serving as [role in student organization]."]

**Fit and Recommendation**

[Student]'s interests in [specific subfield] align closely with the work of [Professor Name(s)] at [University], and I believe [he/she/they] would thrive in your program's [specific feature — collaborative culture, computational resources, interdisciplinary structure]. Of the [number] undergraduates I have supervised in [number] years, I would place [Student] in the top [percentage] — comparable to [former student], who is now [current position/institution].

I recommend [Student] enthusiastically and in the strongest possible terms. Please do not hesitate to contact me at [email] or [phone] if I can provide further information.

Sincerely,

[Signature]
[Your Name]
[Title]
[Institution]

---

**A few notes for adapting this:**

- **Specificity beats superlatives.** One vivid anecdote outweighs three paragraphs of "hardworking and dedicated."
- **Establish your basis for comparison.** "Top 5% of students I've taught in 15 years" is far more useful to a committee than "excellent."
- **State your relationship and its duration up front** — committees discount letters from writers who clearly don't know the student well.
- **Address weaknesses briefly if they're visible** on the transcript; silence can look like avoidance.
- **Tailor the fit paragraph to each program.** Naming specific faculty signals that the application is considered, not scattershot.

If you tell me the student's field, your relationship to them, and two or three specific things they've done, I can produce a tighter, fully customized draft.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Here's the same letter recast for a reader who already has the file — a colleague in the target program who has seen the CV, transcript, and writing sample, and may have met the student at a visit day. The rhetorical job changes completely: nothing needs introducing, so the letter's value lies in calibration, candor, and the things that don't appear on paper.

---

**[Your Name]**
[Title], [Department], [Institution]
[Email] | [Phone]

[Date]

Dear [Colleague's First Name],

You've got [Student]'s file, so I'll skip the recitation and give you what the file can't.

**Calibration.** [Student] is the strongest undergraduate researcher to come through my group since [former student], who you may remember is now [position, institution]. That's [number] years and roughly [number] students. I don't make that comparison casually, and I'd make it again if you asked me in five years.

**What the transcript understates.** The [grade/course] in [Course] is real, and it's not what you might assume. [He/She/They] was [reason — e.g., "carrying twenty hours a week at a job through that semester" / "taking the graduate section as a sophomore and competing with fourth-year students"]. The trajectory afterward is the signal; the single data point isn't.

**What the CV overstates.** The [Journal] manuscript lists [him/her/them] second, but the [specific contribution — e.g., "segmentation pipeline and the entire supplementary analysis"] is [his/hers/theirs]. I wrote the framing and did very little else. Conversely, I'd discount the [conference/poster line] — that was a low bar and everyone in the lab presented.

**The thing that actually persuades me.** [Specific episode, told tightly — e.g., "Last spring our central result failed to replicate across three trials. I was prepared to shelve the project. [Student] came back inside two weeks with a literature review, a candidate confounder we'd both missed, and a control experiment already designed. [He/She/They] was right. That redirection is the paper."] I've watched a lot of talented students go quiet when a result collapses. [He/She/They] got louder and more organized. That's the disposition that finishes a dissertation.

**Where [he/she/they] will need managing.** [Honest limitation — e.g., "[Student] under-communicates when stuck and will burn a week before asking. I've pushed on this and it's improved, but a hands-off advisor would be a bad match. [He/She/They] also writes a first draft that buries the argument on page four — fixable, and [he/she/they] takes edits without ego, which is more than half the battle."] I mention this because you'll find out in year one anyway, and I'd rather you hear it from me.

**Fit.** [He/She/They] should be working with [Name] on [problem], not [Name] on [problem] — the interests look adjacent on paper but the methods aren't, and I think [he/she/they] knows it. Worth asking directly if you interview.

Short version: I'd take [him/her/them] in my own group if [he/she/they] weren't leaving, and I think [he/she/they] will be a credit to your program. Happy to talk by phone if that's more useful than more paragraphs.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

**What changed and why:**

- **No introductions, no summary of credentials.** A reader with the file experiences recapitulation as a waste of their time — and as evidence the writer has nothing firsthand to add.
- **Comparative ranking moved to the top.** For an informed reader, calibration against named predecessors is the single most valuable thing a letter provides, because it's the one judgment only the writer can make.
- **Added a section correcting the record in both directions.** Telling a colleague what the CV *inflates* buys enormous credibility for everything else in the letter. A committee that doesn't know you can't reward that; a colleague who does will.
- **Added a candid limitation.** In the first version this would read as sabotage. Here it reads as professional honesty between peers who will both be accountable for the outcome.
- **Specific advising recommendation.** Only possible when you can assume the reader knows the department's internal landscape.
- **Compressed by roughly half, and the register dropped** — contractions, direct address, a closing offer to talk. Informed readers want signal density and a human on the other end, not formality.

One caution: this version depends on an actual relationship with the recipient and on your willingness to stake your own reputation. If you're not confident the reader will read your candor as candor, use the first version and add only the calibration paragraph.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

---

**[Your Name]** | [Title], [Department], [Institution] | [Email]

[Date]

Dear [Colleague's First Name],

[Student] is the strongest undergraduate researcher to come through my group since [former student], now [position, institution] — that's [number] students over [number] years. Take [him/her/them].

You have the file, so three things it doesn't tell you.

The [Journal] manuscript lists [him/her/them] second, but the [specific contribution] is entirely [his/hers/theirs]. I wrote the framing and little else.

Last spring our central result failed across three replicate trials and I was ready to shelve the project. [Student] came back in two weeks with a candidate confounder we'd both missed and a control experiment already designed. [He/She/They] was right. That redirection is the paper. I've watched plenty of talented students go quiet when a result collapses; this one got louder and better organized.

The caveat: [he/she/they] under-communicates when stuck and will burn a week before asking for help. It's improved under pressure from me, but a hands-off advisor would be the wrong match. Worth steering toward [Name] rather than [Name] — the interests look adjacent on paper, the methods aren't.

I'd keep [him/her/them] in my own group if [he/she/they] weren't leaving. Call me if that's faster.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

**What went and why:**

- **Verdict moved to the first sentence.** Everything after it now functions as support rather than buildup.
- **Section headers cut.** At this length they'd outnumber the content.
- **Transcript defense dropped** — it's the least load-bearing item, and a reader with the file can ask.
- **One anecdote kept, told faster.** The replication story does more work than the other three points combined, so it survives at nearly full length while everything around it compresses.
- **Caveat and fit advice merged** into a single practical paragraph, since both answer the same question: how do we place this person?

If you need it shorter still, the CV-correction paragraph is the next to go.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

---

**[Your Name]** | [Title], [Department], [Institution] | [Email]

[Date]

Dear [Colleague's First Name],

[Student] is the strongest undergraduate researcher to come through my group since [former student], now [position, institution] — that's [number] students over [number] years. Take [him/her/them].

You have the file, so three things it doesn't tell you.

The [Journal] manuscript lists [him/her/them] second, but the [specific contribution] is entirely [his/hers/theirs]. I wrote the framing and little else.

Last spring the project hit a wall and I was ready to shelve it. [Student] came back inside two weeks with a candidate explanation we'd both missed and a control experiment already designed. I've watched plenty of talented students go quiet when a project stalls; this one got louder and better organized.

The caveat: [he/she/they] under-communicates when stuck and will burn a week before asking for help. It's improved under pressure from me, but a hands-off advisor would be the wrong match. Worth steering toward [Name] rather than [Name] — the interests look adjacent on paper, the methods aren't.

I'd keep [him/her/them] in my own group if [he/she/they] weren't leaving. Call me if that's faster.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

**What I removed:** the failure across three replicate trials, "[He/She/They] was right," and "that redirection is the paper" — all four were assertions about what the work showed or produced. I also changed "when a result collapses" to "when a project stalls" so the surrounding sentence doesn't reintroduce the claim by implication. Everything else is untouched.

**Two things to check on your end:**

The anecdote now describes the student's *response* to a setback rather than the setback's outcome, which is still a real recommendation — initiative and diagnostic instinct — but it no longer lands with vindication. If that's too thin for the placement, tell me and I can build the paragraph around a different behavior that doesn't touch results at all: how [he/she/they] runs a lit review, mentors junior students, or handles edits.

I left the [Journal] manuscript reference in place, since it's a claim about authorship rather than findings. But if your constraint stems from the paper being embargoed or the results being unreleased, the mere reference to a manuscript under review may also be a problem. Say the word and I'll cut it — the CV-correction paragraph was already the next thing on the chopping block, so the letter tightens rather than suffers.
